extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, patent practitioners, and applicants
extracted.subtask_short: MPEP patentability and prior art guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Official USPTO examination guidance on evaluating patentability and prior art issues, including special procedures for claims relating to tax strategies and detailed standards for drawings, patents/applications, printed publications, electronic sources, and public accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construe claims per MPEP §2111
rubrics_metrics.description: Construe the claim in accordance with MPEP § 2111 et seq.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow claim construction principles in MPEP § 2111 prior to substantive patentability analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze claim for 35 U.S.C. 101 and 112 compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze the claim for compliance with 35 U.S.C. 101 and 112 in accordance with current guidance, which is unaffected by this provision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform applicability checks for subject matter eligibility and specification/claim requirements (written description, enablement, definiteness) per existing USPTO guidance before applying tax-strategy-specific rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify tax strategy claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify any limitations relating to a tax strategy, as defined above (note the listed exclusions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether claim limitations pertain to tax strategies, especially those suitable for use with tax-favored structures (employee benefit plans, tax-exempt organizations, or other entities requiring particular structure/operation to obtain tax consequences). See MPEP § 2124.01 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax strategy limitations treated as within prior art for 35 U.S.C. 102/103
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the claim in view of the prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103, treating any limitations relating to a tax strategy as being within the prior art, and not as a patentable difference between the claim and the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accord patentable weight to tax-strategy limitations when assessing novelty/obviousness; analogous to the treatment of printed matter limitations (see MPEP § 2112.01).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use form paragraph 7.06.01 for tax strategy limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph 7.06.01 may be used to indicate claim limitation(s) interpreted as a tax strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form text: 'Claim limitation "[1]" has been interpreted as a strategy for reducing, avoiding, or deferring tax liability ("tax strategy") pursuant to Section 14 of the Leahy‑Smith America Invents Act. Accordingly, this claim limitation is being treated as being within the prior art and is insufficient to differentiate the invention of claim [2] from the prior art.' Examiner Note: recite the limitation in bracket 1, insert claim number(s) in bracket 2; see MPEP § 2124.01 for more information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-implemented methods: give weight to technical features, not tax strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: A computer-implemented method that is deemed novel and non-obvious would not be affected by this provision even if used for a tax purpose. However, a prior art computer-implemented method would not become non-obvious by implementing a novel and non-obvious tax strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Software-related inventions under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103: claim limitations directed solely to enabling individuals to file income tax returns or assist with managing finances should be given patentable weight, except that claim limitations directed to a tax strategy should not be given patentable weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings/pictures can anticipate if they clearly show claimed structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings and pictures can anticipate claims if they clearly show the structure which is claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The picture must show all the claimed structural features and how they are put together. The origin of the drawing is immaterial. Evaluate drawings for what they reasonably disclose and suggest to one of ordinary skill in the art. See In re Mraz; Jockmus v. Leviton; In re Aslanian.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportions in drawings not evidence if drawings not to scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportions of features in a drawing are not evidence of actual proportions when drawings are not to scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the reference does not disclose drawings are to scale and is silent as to dimensions, arguments based on measurement of drawings have little value. However, the textual description combined with drawings can be relied upon. See Hockerson‑Halberstadt v. Avia Group Int’l; In re Wright.

rubrics_metrics.name: The name 'patent' alone does not make a document prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: What a foreign country designates to be a patent may not be a patent for purposes of rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) and (b); it is the substance of the rights conferred and the way information within the 'patent' is controlled that is determinative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the actual public availability and rights conferred, not merely the label 'patent.' See In re Ekenstam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secret patents: not prior art until publicly available; pre‑AIA 102(d) exception
rubrics_metrics.description: A secret patent is not available as a reference under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or pre‑AIA 102(a) or (b) until it is available to the public but it may be available under pre‑AIA 102(d) as of the grant date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent is sufficiently available to the public for 102(a) if laid open for public inspection or disseminated in printed form. Secrecy after grant does not affect use under pre‑AIA 102(d). See In re Carlson; In re Kathawala; MPEP § 2135 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date a patent is available as a reference
rubrics_metrics.description: The date the patent is available as a reference is generally the date the sovereign formally bestows patent rights to the applicant (the date the patent becomes enforceable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception when the patent is secret as of the date rights are awarded (see In re Ekenstam). See MPEP § 901.05 for foreign patent dating.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a patent is used as a 'patent' (not a 'publication'), examiner may rely on specification details
rubrics_metrics.description: When the patented document is used as a patent and not as a publication, the examiner may use any information provided in the specification which relates to the subject matter of the patented claims when making a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(a) or pre‑AIA 102(a), (b) or (d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unclaimed details in the specification can be relied upon if they relate to the patented claims; courts treat 'invention ... patented' broadly to include disclosed aspects. See Ex parte Ovist; In re Kathawala; In re Fuge discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandoned applications are prior art only when publicly disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: An abandoned patent application may become evidence of prior art only when it has been appropriately disclosed (e.g., referenced in the disclosure of another patent, in a publication, or by voluntary disclosure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An abandoned application becomes available as prior art only as of the date the public gains access. See Lee Pharmaceutical v. Kreps; 37 CFR 1.14(a)(1)(ii) and (iv).

rubrics_metrics.name: Canceled matter: unavailable for certain rejections but may be available in others
rubrics_metrics.description: Canceled matter in the application file of a U.S. patent or application cannot be relied upon in a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canceled matter only becomes available as prior art as of the date the application file history becomes available to the public; however, canceled matter may be available under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) in some circumstances. See Ex parte Stalego; In re Lund; see MPEP §§ 2136.02, 2136.03, 2154.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laid open foreign applications may constitute 'published' documents if publicly accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: When the specification is not issued in printed form but is announced in an official journal and anyone can inspect or obtain copies, it is sufficiently accessible to the public to constitute a 'publication' within 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or pre‑AIA 102(a) and (b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accessibility determines status; technological advances increase reproducibility and accessibility. Examiner should confirm publication date by reviewing a copy of the laid open application. See In re Wyer; Ex parte Haller; MPEP § 901.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pending U.S. applications: confidentiality and limited uses
rubrics_metrics.description: All pending U.S. applications are preserved in confidence except for published applications, reissue applications, and applications opened to public inspection under 37 CFR 1.11(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejections relying on copending unpublished applications may be proper in some circumstances (e.g., provisional double patenting, common assignee/inventor issues). See MPEP §§ 804, 2120.01, 2136 et seq., 2154 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication test: public accessibility to interested skilled persons
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference is a 'printed publication' if it has been disseminated or otherwise made available to the extent that persons interested and ordinarily skilled in the art, exercising reasonable diligence, can locate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination is a legal conclusion based on facts and circumstances (case‑by‑case). The party asserting prior art bears the burden of proving public accessibility. See In re Wyer; Blue Calypso; Kyocera Wireless; Suffolk Techs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic/Internet publications can be 'printed publications' if accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: An electronic publication, including an online database or Internet publication (discussion group, forum, digital video, social media post), is a 'printed publication' provided the publication was accessible to persons concerned with the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office policy requires recordation of search results and retention of office copies for internet sources. Electronic documents must be proven disseminated or otherwise accessible to interested skilled persons. See In re Wyer; Amazon.com v. Barnesandnoble.com; In re Epstein; Suffolk Tech v. AOL/Google.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date of availability for internet/online disclosures equals posting date (absent evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art disclosures on the Internet or an online database are considered publicly available as of the date the item was publicly posted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the publication does not include a publication or retrieval date, it cannot be relied upon under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or pre‑AIA 102(a) or (b) absent other evidence; examiners may ask STIC to find the earliest date. See MPEP § 901.06(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of teachings relied upon from electronic sources and abstracts
rubrics_metrics.description: An electronic publication may be relied upon for all that it would have reasonably suggested to one having ordinary skill in the art; however, if an electronic document is merely an abstract of a patent or printed publication, only the text of the abstract may be relied upon to support a rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When electronic and paper versions differ appreciably, each may need to be cited and relied upon for what they disclose. See MPEP § 2121.01 and § 2123.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wayback Machine captures as prima facie evidence of public accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art obtained via the Wayback Machine® sets forth a prima facie case that the art was publicly accessible at the date and time provided in the time stamp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The burden then shifts to the applicant to challenge authenticity, reliability, or accessibility of the archived information. Retain records as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media can be prior art but requires case‑by‑case accessibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media websites (YouTube, Twitter, Facebook, public forums) can be sources of prior art provided the public accessibility requirements are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess factors such as where posted, privacy restrictions, how long it was posted, and whether it was indexed for searching. Some social media sites are not archived by Wayback Machine; timestamps on sites may need careful scrutiny. See MPEP § 707.05(e) for citation formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: No need to prove anyone actually viewed a publicly accessible reference
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no need to prove that someone actually looked at a publication when that publication is accessible to the public through a library or patent office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If accessibility is proved, there is no requirement to show that particular members of the public actually received the information. See In re Wyer; In re Hall; Jazz Pharm. v. Amneal; Constant v. AMD.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of public accessibility: indexing, cataloging, and discoverability matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A thesis placed in a university library or a document in an online database may be prior art if sufficiently accessible to the public; indexing and cataloging practices are relevant to accessibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: In re Hall (thesis indexed/shelved properly = prior art) vs In re Cronyn (poor shelving/indexing = not accessible). Indexing is a factor but not required; evaluate technical searchability and discoverability (see Voter Verified; Acceleration Bay).

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral presentation can be a printed publication if written copies are distributed without restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper orally presented in a forum open to all interested persons constitutes a 'printed publication' if written copies are disseminated without restriction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oral presentations at scientific meetings or demonstrations at trade shows may be prior art where written copies or unrestricted dissemination occurred. See Massachusetts Institute of Technology v. AB Fortia.
